reverse_outline.summary: What the part covers: the listing domain model and its subdomains
Business cost of weak listing models: unfindable listings, stale contacts, misbilled sellers
Downstream systems copy the listing, so its shape decides whether copies agree
Three key points: small reference-holding aggregate, governed reference data, privacy and legal weight in the model
Failure patterns the part fixes: category straitjacket, attribute junkyard, ghost inventory
Bridge from Part I and the familiar decay of a once-modeled listing table
Thesis: listing as an offer, a small aggregate surrounded by five contracted subdomains
Why the six chapters come in dependency order, plus a roadmap of the rest of the page
Lead-in to the chapter table of questions and when to read
How Part III and later parts build on and read these models as contracts
Veldmark's starting mess and its per-chapter modeling decisions with dates
The three recurring examples the chapters test decisions on
Synthesis of the part's outcome and pointer to start with the listing aggregate chapter

results.finding: cause_effect: 'The rest of the book builds on these six models' carries the models into their consequence for later parts.

results.finding: example: 'Veldmark ... shows these models becoming contracts' picks up the contracts framing of the previous section.

results.draft_locus: The Veldmark thread -> Where to begin
results.finding: conclusion_summary: 'Read together, the six chapters replace...' opens the synthesis.

Both readers describe the order as why -> what -> where next with the chapter order stated as dependency order, which agrees with the declared large_to_small with prerequisite_order for the chapters; neither marks any section's position unclear. Points both raised but not counted as lost-thread: Tradeyard, Ingrid Halvorsen and the three recurring examples (A 3f/3h, B 3h/3j) and Veldmark named in the roadmap (A 3e) are on audience.already_knows and linked to meet-veldmark; the Ghost Inventory 'deadline' (A 3i, B 3b) both readers understood, and its mechanism is chapter content (non-goal).

results.quote: Sellers and accounts come last: they hold the seller facts the others point to.
results.finding: Both readers report that this reason contradicts the paragraph's own principle 'each needs the one before': if the other models point to seller facts, they need sellers first, so the stated reason argues for putting sellers early. The draft copies the reason from the spec (thesis claim 'ending with sellers and accounts because they own what the earlier chapters only point to' and p03's controlling idea), so the fix is a spec decision: give a reason for sellers last that fits the dependency principle, or soften the principle.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader B, item 3(f) (same sentence, same contradiction; A item 3(b))

results.quote: Media comes before location: location hides a private seller's precise point, which a photo's GPS coordinates would reveal unless media strips them.
results.finding: Both readers needed a second read: the sentence's subject is location while its conclusion is about media. Lead with the dependency (media strips photo GPS, which location's privacy relies on), then the order.

results.quote: The category selects the rules for the rest, and attributes are bound to a category.
results.finding: Both readers paused on 'the rest': the remaining chapters or the rest of the listing's data. Name what the category selects (the rules for attributes, fees and facets, as the spec's how_why says).

results.quote: This part argues that a listing is **an offer about a thing, not the thing itself**. The aggregate stays small and strict.
results.finding: Both readers looked for the link from 'an offer about a thing' to 'therefore a small aggregate with the thing's descriptors outside it' and did not find it; the bolded thesis reads as a slogan beside the argument. One clause saying why an offer stays small would close the gap.

results.quote: Seller edits and platform expiry share one publication state; enforcement (trust and safety's holds and blocks) is a separate overlay.
results.finding: Both readers call this the densest sentence on the page and had to re-read it to see that publication state and enforcement overlay are two separate dimensions and why that matters to the small-aggregate claim. The spec's gloss is present; the sentence needs splitting or one more phrase, not a new term.

results.quote: Ingrid Halvorsen's team decides, by chapter rather than by date:
results.finding: Both readers stopped at the out-of-order dates (Veldmark Place, May 2027, listed fourth) despite the 'by chapter rather than by date' note, B checking whether a date was wrong. The chapter order is the spec's and is right; the draft can make the note land where the snag is (beside the May 2027 item, or say that the dates do not follow chapter order).

results.quote: Media and location then govern photos and places as owned, versioned data.
results.finding: Reader B only: the sentence says what the two chapters do, not what they need from the attribute chapter, so this step of 'each needs the one before' is not justified. The spec's p03 controlling idea has the same gap.

results.quote: Begin with [[listing-aggregate]], which defines the aggregate.
results.finding: Reader B only: near-tautological; the roadmap's better reason (it decides what sits inside the listing and what is only a reference) could be reused.

does_not_know terms are handled as the spec requires: enforcement overlay (glossed as trust and safety's holds and blocks, apart from the one publication state), gazetteer (register of named places), trader status (whether a seller acts as a business) and entitlements (what a seller has paid for) are glossed; precision policy and attribute dictionaries are named and left to their chapters; taxonomy release and content-addressed asset are not used. Tradeyard, Ingrid Halvorsen, Veldmark and the recurring examples, which the cold readers found unexplained, are on already_knows. The readers' difficulty with 'overlay' is recorded under flow_is_followable (KEY POINTS bullet), not here.
The introduction opens on a concrete example (the two-hundred-column ads table), bridges from Part I and states a disputable thesis; none of the five weak patterns.
The closing synthesises, states the so-what and the test, and hands off to listing-aggregate without a new idea, an 'in conclusion' opener or a mere rephrasing.
'replace the two-hundred-column ads table with a small aggregate and five contracts, so every system that copies a listing copies the same meaning' gives the synthesis and the so-what.
The closing calls back to the two-hundred-column ads table of the first paragraph and restates the test (who owns each part, how it is versioned, which systems copy it).

The intro reader predicted a chapter table of the six chapters in order with the reason for the order, then how the part connects to the book, then what Veldmark decides, which is both roadmap promises and the page as written. Its side notes (the 1 + 5 count, 'after the table' before the table is introduced) did not stop the prediction.

The reader named all six chapters in order with their questions (what a listing is, invariants and lifecycle; a category tree that can change; attributes validated, searched and evolved; ingesting, storing, moderating and serving images; location for search, maps and privacy; the people and organizations that supply listings), matching expected.
The reader opened attribute-schemas for the empty frame-size filter and sellers-and-accounts for the franchise branches, as expected.

The reader gave Part III (forms and feeds, enrichment, duplicates, publication) and that search indexes the attribute schemas, trust and safety writes the enforcement overlay and entitlements attach to accounts, matching expected.
